newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Price hikes to aid small China refineries - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Price hikes to aid small China refineries - analysts.

text.p: Domestic price increases for refined petroleum products in China have done little to improve profit margins for export-oriented coastal refineries, but smaller inland refineries should benefit, industry sources said on Wednesday.

China, through state-owned refiner SINOPEC, on October 18 raised ex-refinery prices for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) to 1,200 yuan from 800 yuan; diesel fuel to 1,990 yuan from 1,900 and fuel oil to 1,350 yuan from 1,300.

Industry sources said the new prices would benefit smaller and medium-sized refineries in the country's interior who can now charge more for refined products in China while still buying domestic crude oil at fixed prices.

But larger refineries along China's coast were unlikely to improve their profit margins because they buy most of their crude on the international market, where prices recently reached five-year highs.
China's refining capacity is about 4.1 million barrels per day (bpd), about one million of which comes from coastal refineries.
But utilization is only about 70 percent, analysts say.
Chinese crude sells for 1,000-1,200 yuan per tonne ($16-$19 per barrel) to domestic buyers compared with Asian benchmark Dubai, which fetches around (1,260 yuan per tonne) or $20.30 per barrel.

Sources at coastal refineries in Fujian and Guangzhou in southern China told Reuters world oil prices have risen "too fast and too much" compared to the almost negligible adjustment in domestic prices for refined oil products.
One trader said international crude prices had risen four times faster than those of domestic oil products.
"Gasoil prices should be raised by at least 150 yuan instead of only 90 yuan for refining to be profitable," said a trader at a Chinese oil firm.
International benchmark Brent crude hit a five-year peak of $25.06 per barrel on October 15. Prices have eased since, but refiners said prices are still high compared to those domestic crude.

A SINOPEC source said he expected the state refiner's profits to improve due to the price changes. SINOPEC operates about 39 refineries in China and is responsible for more than 95 percent of the country's oil and chemicals production.
The rise in product prices still left ex-refinery prices lower than international product prices, so traders said they doubted the new prices would spur more demand for imports.
SINOPEC sources said there were no immediate plans to adjust oil product prices again. But a CNPC official said China planned to raise domestic crude prices in the second half of 1997.
